output.headline: Transatlantic partnership leads to swift arrest in security case
output.bodyHtml:
A US soldier with alleged links to Russia has been arrested by British counter-terrorism police.

The man, 41, was arrested as part of an investigation by counter-terrorism police, working closely with US authorities, the US military and the FBI, London counter-terrorism police said.

US army counterintelligence command said the allegations related to a “senior soldier”.

The soldier was based at Imjin barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato’s allied rapid reaction corps.

The man was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday on suspicion of offences under section one and section three of the National Security Act: assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.

He remains in custody at a London police station.

As part of the investigation, officers were carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said.

The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement the arrest “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies”.

“This matter shows that partnerships are essential to protect our countries and I want to express my thanks to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence and the US Army Counterintelligence Command for their outstanding work.”

He added: “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.

“This includes 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests from this FBI over the last 21 months – a 53% increase.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter-terrorism policing investigations.

Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved.”

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing.

“We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security.”

Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US army counterintelligence command, said the alleged conduct “of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent”.

He added: “I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office.”
output.standfirst: Counter-terrorism police, working closely with the FBI and US army counterintelligence, arrested a senior US soldier, 41, near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, in a case the FBI director called a matter of 'utmost concern'
output.progress: UK and US counter-terrorism police, the FBI and army counterintelligence are jointly investigating and say they will take robust action against any suspected threat.

output.headline: US charges Iranian operative over foiled plot to bomb UK air base
output.bodyHtml:
US federal prosecutors have said that an Iranian operative jailed in New York was responsible for the foiled attack on a UK air force base where American B-1 bombers were stationed.

Five men from London were arrested in the village of Whelford, near RAF Fairford, on 27 September on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences, after a farmer reported vans blocking a road near the base while on her way back from a party.

A new indictment alleged that Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in custody and then transmitted plans – using coded messages in calls to his family – to two co-conspirators to buy large quantities of chemicals that could be used as explosives in an attack on the RAF Fairford base in September.

Al-Saadi, who was accused of being associated with Kata’ib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was said to have planned the attack as retribution for the US war in Iran.

He had already been charged for his alleged links to 18 terrorist attacks in Europe and for allegedly planning to bomb a synagogue in New York as well, according to a statement by the southern district of New York.

He was already imprisoned when he began planning the attack, according to the indictment, which said he then transmitted his plans by using coded messages in calls to his family to pass on to Mohsen Mohajeri, an operative of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and another Iranian, Mohammad Ali al-Hassani.

Al-Hassani then tasked others with surveilling the Fairford RAF base and with procuring vans and barrels of fuel, and researching the purchase of chemical accelerants and metallic objects to be used as shrapnel, the indictment claimed.

RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers and was used by the US during its bombing campaign against Iran. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement noting RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers and saying any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said the US attorney Jamie McDonald. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas.”

“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical – it is very real,” he added.
output.standfirst: US prosecutors have charged Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, already in custody, after authorities said they foiled his coded-message plot to bomb RAF Fairford, the UK base for US bombers, as retribution for the Iran war
output.progress: Prosecutors say they foiled the bombing plot before it could be carried out, and five men were arrested near the base in September.

output.headline: Judge dismisses Trump's unfair-trade claim against the BBC
output.bodyHtml:
Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

And the judge determined that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

The BBC released a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

The judge noted the significance of the documentary’s editing decision, which spliced together comments made by Trump that were nearly 55 minutes apart, something the BBC has apologized for.

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” he wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The judge continued: “Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

The judge noted past errors in the broadcaster’s coverage and wrote that “such examples can be said to be probative of BBC’s state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC’s non-action toward false statements about Trump. Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump.”

The judge also wrote that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

Trump heralded the ruling on Truth Social, calling it a “huge victory”. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump said.

In late October, a Florida magistrate judge ruled that Trump will have to sit for a deposition conducted by lawyers for the BBC by 11 December or else he could be hit with sanctions.
output.standfirst: A judge dismissed one of Trump's claims against the BBC, but ruled his $10bn defamation suit over an edited Panorama documentary can proceed to trial, where he must still prove actual malice and real damages
output.progress: The BBC says it remains confident in its position and will continue to defend itself through the proper legal process.

context.text: The BBC is also seeking to subpoena Trump's children and son-in-law for testimony as it builds its defence against the lawsuit.

output.headline: More victims come forward to police as judge praises their bravery
output.bodyHtml:
Police have received further criminal allegations against Russell Brand since the start of his trial.

The Metropolitan police said several people had been in contact during and since the conclusion of the 51-year-old’s rape and sexual assault case.

The force said those who had been in contact had either provided further information or reported potential criminal allegations.

A spokesperson said: “Several people have contacted the investigation team during and since the trial to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation. Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing inquiries.”

Brand was jailed for 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, including at their workplaces.

The judge in Brand’s trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the bravery of the women who had come forward with evidence that led to his conviction.

But the way the victims were questioned by the disgraced comedian’s legal representative, Ian Winter KC, has been criticised in recent days.

Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, described the cross-examination as “depressing”, saying she believed the courts had “long gone past that sort of culture”.

Powell, who is also the education secretary, said that she regretted a meeting the former party leader Ed Miliband had with Brand in 2015 when she was Labour’s campaign chief.

Powell was asked on LBC radio about Brand’s defence in court, during which Winter suggested he must be innocent because none of his victims had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”. Winter also said the anal rape of a 21-year-old woman was a “short and momentary failure” where “he did not respect her consent”.

Asked if that was reminiscent of the attitude of the 1950s, Powell said she had been shocked at some of what took place in the courtroom, while praising the judge’s words. “I found reading some of that incredibly sort of depressing. I thought we’d long gone past that sort of culture and that phase of things.

“And the judge’s remarks were also incredibly powerful in sentencing: that it doesn’t matter what you wear, how you behaved, how drunk you are, you know, you have the right to give your consent or not give your consent. And if it’s not given, then that is rape and that is a sexual offence, pure and simple.”

The BBC’s director general, Matt Brittin, wrote to the corporation’s staff to say that he wanted to ensure any concerns raised about workplace culture were heard “at the highest level”. His intervention followed criticism that Brand’s troubling behaviour had not been challenged properly during his time at the broadcaster.

Brittin said in his email that there had been valid criticism levelled at the media industry over its workplace culture after Brand’s conviction and recent allegations of antisemitism at the BBC.

Brand, who had stints as a presenter on BBC 6 Music and Radio 2 in 2006 and 2007, once joked on air about exposing himself to a woman moments before his show was broadcast. He also described one BBC boss, who has since left the broadcaster, as “incredibly tolerant” of his behaviour.

Brittin said the BBC and the wider media industry had made progress in improving culture, but that there was “still more to do to engage with staff and represent their views and concerns at the highest level”.

Brittin said he was looking at changes to improve culture that could be made immediately and as part of the next BBC charter being discussed with ministers.

The BBC published a review in 2025 that found some staff had felt unable to speak out because of Brand’s status and power. The corporation repeated its apology this week.

After the treatment of some of Brand’s accusers during his trial, Powell said the government had taken steps in guidance to challenge myths about rape and victim-blaming in court. “But clearly, a lot more needs to be done because I think many of us were really shocked that that could still take place in a courtroom today,” she said.

At sentencing, the judge criticised Brand, saying the women had been subjected to additional suffering because of the conduct in court “on your instructions”.

“Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent,” he said.

Powell said she and Miliband regretted that he had done an interview with Brand in 2015 during the hype around Revolution, Brand’s book on politics. At the time the interview took place, Brand had resigned from his BBC Radio 2 show for leaving a series of lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs’ answerphone about his granddaughter.

“It was a long time ago, obviously, and had I or Ed Miliband or anybody at the time had any sense at all that this was someone who was a sexual predator, who was involved in these sorts of crimes,” she told Sky News, anyone who was involved in promoting him would “look back and really regret that, knowing today what we now know”.

Asked about her role in setting up the interview, Powell said she had not understood the full extent of his sexual conduct that was already in the public domain – such as in his autobiography. “If there was any suggestion at all we were dealing with someone who was a known sexual predator at the time then, of course, no one would have done that.

“But as I say, he was a well-known public figure. Lots of people, from Hollywood to the BBC to many others, gave this person a very, very powerful platform.”
output.standfirst:
The Met says several people have come forward with new information or allegations since Russell Brand's trial, as the judge praised the bravery of the women whose evidence led to his conviction for rape and sexual assault

  • Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
output.progress: The BBC's director general has pledged to address workplace culture concerns, and the government has introduced guidance to challenge rape myths in court.

output.headline: Oil price falls to its lowest since August as Trump eases Iran tensions
output.bodyHtml:
Brent crude oil has persistently traded at more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks – compared with about $70 before the war – but on Tuesday it traded below $90 at one point, the lowest since 31 August, after Donald Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”.

The Bank of England is risking higher interest rates for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation, according to leading thinktank.

In a searing critique of the central bank’s tactics, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) said a timid increase in interest rates last week was likely to mean inflation staying above the Bank’s 2% target until at least 2030.

The thinktank said inflation was likely to become a more persistent feature of the UK economy unless the Bank took tougher action.

The Bank’s monetary policy committee increased the cost of borrowing from 3.75% to 4% last week and hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

The director of the Niesr, David Aikman, urged the Bank of England to be more aggressive in tackling inflation, saying all the ingredients were in place for workers to demand inflation-linked salary rises.

“Inflation is set to rise above 4% in the new year, just as most pay awards for 2027 are being agreed, so the risk that it becomes embedded is rising.

“One further quarter-point rise is unlikely to be enough, and the longer the MPC waits, the more it will eventually need to do.”

UK inflation stands at 3.5%, well above the Bank’s 2% target, driven higher by the soaring cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have risen sharply since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

Investors, however, reined in their enthusiasm after US inflation climbed by 0.4 percentage points from September to October, revealing that high oil and gas prices were continuing to drive up costs. The S&P 500 index of leading US companies was down 0.9% by early afternoon on Wall Street.

The Niesr said its forecasts for growth in the UK and the global economy were based on oil prices at $105 a barrel. However, it cautioned that while prices had dropped, continued difficulties shipping and refining meant consumer prices would decline slowly.

Stephen Millard, an economist at the institute, said the lower oil price was also dependent on Trump sticking to his new policy. “We’ve seen him change his mind before,” he said.

The Niesr expects the UK economy to grow by 1.6% this year, but by only 0.9% in 2028 as high inflation, high interest rates and tight government spending take a toll on consumer and business confidence.

The chancellor, John Healey, was criticised for deferring difficult decisions in the budget last month, which the institute said would leave a £30bn hole in the government’s finances if the pattern of doing so over the last decade was repeated next year.

Aikman said financial markets would punish the Treasury by raising the price of loans to the UK if it became clear that government spending was going to soar in areas such as defence without savings being made elsewhere.

He said there was a “double whammy” from higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs that was not being addressed.

“Those pressures reflect global developments and cannot be avoided,” he said. “How monetary and fiscal policy respond to them is a domestic choice, and on both fronts decisions are being deferred.”
output.standfirst: Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel on Tuesday, its lowest since August, after Trump downplayed military action against Iran, as thinktank Niesr said the Bank of England's rate rise may leave inflation elevated until 2030
output.progress: Oil prices have eased after Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran, though economists caution the relief may not last.

context.text: City economists say the sharp rate rises markets expect are unlikely, with the Bank of England possibly 'sounding the all clear' by spring and cutting rates again by the end of 2027.

output.headline: Casey sets out a 'new settlement' as ministers fast-track social care reform
output.bodyHtml:
Casey is expected to call for a “new settlement” for care, “one based on values I still believe this country shares: decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves”.

Successive governments in England have been “asleep at the wheel” on social care, leaving the system to grow as a chaotic patchwork of local services with no clear vision, Louise Casey, the head of the social care commission, is to warn.

Lady Casey, who is preparing proposals for a big review of adult social care, will say the result is that in effect “no one is in charge” of a system that provides vital services for millions of vulnerable people.

People’s experiences of care have varied depending on where they live, with different standards, assessment processes and waiting times, while the private care sector has grown dominant and regulation of services has often been ineffectual, she will say.

She will add that England has no clear “system stewardship” for social care, making it difficult for governments to target improvements to services or translate policy into practice, unlike in comparable countries such as France, Germany and Japan.

Casey’s latest robust critique of adult social care, together with her view that the system faces a “moment of reckoning”, has additional force given Andy Burnham’s ambitions to introduce a new national care service and reform care funding and the workforce.

The prime minister has embraced the Casey review, accelerating its completion to next year – 12 months quicker than envisaged by the Starmer government – with the expectation that a national care service plan will be in Labour’s next election manifesto.

He has already announced he would use savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock, starting in the next parliament, to target investment into a care service based on the Scottish approach of free personal care, with individuals paying for “bed and board” costs.

Speaking at the annual national children and adult services conference on Wednesday, Casey will also say she has written to the Covid-19 inquiry agreeing with its findings on social care.

She is expected to say: “The Covid-19 inquiry took apart the argument that a ‘protective ring’ had been thrown around care homes during the pandemic. Many old people died without their loved ones by their side. Many care workers left their jobs after what they had seen.

“It is a national shame that this was allowed to happen. It should never happen again.”

The Covid-19 inquiry chair, Heather Hallett, last month described the adult care sector during the pandemic as “something of an afterthought”, with care home residents and staff given insufficient protection. More than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

Casey has drawn on research that highlights how the lack of oversight and a “clear coherent narrative” in English social care is a “significant weakness” in the system, exacerbated by the historic low visibility of social care among successive governments.

The research, by the Nuffield Trust and the Institute for Government, found the lack of clarity in the system made it difficult and slow for policy change to happen. But it warned politicians against embarking on disruptive structural changes without a clear purpose or political determination.

“One last and inescapable point is that successful reform of social care requires political will and bravery to make the choices outlined throughout this report,” it said.

“No amount of reorganisation of governance structures or processes will be sufficient in the absence of political impetus to drive through change and dedicate resources, time and energy to social care. Maintaining social care visibility and priority within the government’s agenda will be essential.”
output.standfirst: Louise Casey will call for a 'new settlement' for care, as the prime minister fast-tracks a national care service plan, after saying that successive governments have left the system a chaotic patchwork with 'no one in charge'
output.progress: The prime minister has accelerated the Casey review and plans to fund new care investment by scrapping the pension triple lock.

output.headline: Jeffries vows to pursue Hegseth impeachment once Democrats control Congress
output.bodyHtml:
House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, had proposed impeaching Hegseth in September, alleging an array of illegal acts, including killing civilians in Iran, launching unauthorized operations in Venezuela and Yemen, and retaliating against a Democratic senator.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.

Tuesday’s vote is unlikely to be the final word on efforts to remove Hegseth from office, after Democrats won decisive majorities in the November midterm elections. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January, has backed the push to impeach Hegseth, accusing the embattled secretary of having “undermined America’s national security”.

In an interview with PBS on Tuesday, Jeffries said he was “a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution”.

“He’s abused his power. He’s undermined our national security. And Pete Hegseth is the architect of this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has made our country less safe and made life more expensive for the American people,” Jeffries told the news outlet.

Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot’ and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”.

“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.

The resolution’s downfall took place hours after Hegseth held a defiant press conference at the Pentagon, where he dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political spectacle” orchestrated by the ousted Kentucky congressman.

Related: What to know about impeachment amid effort to oust US defense secretary Pete Hegseth

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.

The conflict with Iran has proven divisive with Republicans, and ahead of the midterms, small but growing numbers voted with Democrats on war powers resolutions intended to force Trump to bring the hostilities to a close. Warren Davidson, one of the House Republicans who voted for such resolutions, said he nonetheless rejected the idea of impeaching Hegseth.

“It’s an effort to blame-shift on to Hegseth Congress’s failure and President Trump’s decision,” Davidson said in an interview.

“I think Hegseth has been incredibly effective at restoring morale for the active-duty force, restoring the warrior ethos, the proper focus to the military that they exist to fight and win wars.”

The defense secretary, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer, has been one of the most pugnacious members of Trump’s second term cabinet, and taken an unusually heavy handed approach to managing the US military. Hegseth has orchestrated the departure of top generals, blocked the promotions of scores of officers, many of them women and people of color, and implemented new rules that prompted much of the press corps to leave the Pentagon.

He has also become the public face of some of the administration’s most politically costly policies, particularly the Iran war, which has dragged on for months while putting upward pressure on petroleum prices and played into Democrats’s hands in last week’s midterms.

Related: Hegseth lays it on thick for Trump to shave off fallout from Iran war

Massie’s resolution outlined eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, including attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and spurning a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict.

It also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary.

The final two impeachment articles target Hegseth’s involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House.

Had the impeachment resolution passed, it would have had to be approved by the Senate, which Republicans control by a 53-seat margin. It is unclear if it would have had enough votes to pass, or if the Republican leader John Thune would have even put it up for consideration.
output.standfirst: Hakeem Jeffries, likely to become House speaker in January, says he is a 'hard yes' on impeaching Pete Hegseth, after Republicans blocked Thomas Massie's resolution this week, as Trump hailed Hegseth's 'exoneration'
output.progress: Hakeem Jeffries, likely to become House speaker in January, says he backs reviving the push to impeach Hegseth.

output.headline: Opposition pushes reform bills to curb Netanyahu's power as new Knesset convenes
output.bodyHtml:
Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they fail to broker a coalition.

Priorities include setting up a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks and introducing term limits for Israel’s prime ministers, which could block Netanyahu from taking power again. He has ruled Israel for 19 of the last 30 years.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party submitted a series of bills to the Knesset moments after the swearing in, with backing from other opposition parties.

In addition to term limits and the 7 October inquiry, legislation includes several bills designed to revoke the “judicial overhaul” pursued by Netanyahu, which weakened the power of Israel’s judiciary and the attorney general.

Ohana has tabled the vote on a new speaker to replace him for next Tuesday, the latest date possible. The opposition have also nominated candidates to take over key defence and finance committees.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, now has the presidential mandate to try to form a government. If he fails to broker a deal within six weeks, a second candidate – probably Netanyahu – will get a second chance. Further failure is likely to lead to another election.

Netanyahu responded to the swearing in of the new Knesset on Tuesday with a racist attack on two Palestinian-led opposition parties, whose voters were essential to unseating his coalition, calling their lawmakers “terror supporters”.

Eisenkot denounced his speech as a “delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful” exploitation of a state occasion, that showed the prime minister was unfit for office.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, and Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish-Israeli former police chief who ran on the slate of Islamist Ra’am party, both walked out of Netanyahu’s speech in protest.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the country’s population. Netanyahu put attacks on these voters and their parties at the heart of his campaign, and since polling day has promoted groundless accusations of fraud in their communities in a bid to undermine results.

Election officials say there was no evidence of irregularities that affected the election outcome or compromised its integrity.

A period of prolonged, difficult coalition negotiations or even a new round of elections would extend Netanyahu’s hold on power as caretaker prime minister. But if the fractured opposition can make progress on key legislation, his grip on the state would be weakened.

Eisenkot has admitted the path to power is “extraordinarily complex”, because of incompatible election promises made by different parties, but described ousting Netanyahu as a national emergency that could require breaking promises.

At the swearing-in ceremony, the president, Isaac Herzog, warned lawmakers they should do everything in their power to avoid a second election.

“Reach out a hand for compromise, even between ⁠rivals … Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House.“
output.standfirst: Opposition parties moved swiftly to seize the Knesset's agenda, pushing bills for term limits and a 7 October inquiry, after Netanyahu branded Palestinian-led parties 'terror supporters' at the swearing-in, remarks Eisenkot called 'shameful'
output.progress: Eisenkot's party has already submitted bills on term limits, the 7 October inquiry and reversing Netanyahu's judicial overhaul.

output.headline: Markle rearrested within hours of cutting off ankle monitor, officials say
output.bodyHtml:
The estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, has been jailed after US authorities said he cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California.

Thomas Markle, 82, was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said. He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 1.45am on Tuesday, Essayli said.

“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions. We are asking the court to revoke his release and detain him pending trial, and we will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law,” Essayli said.

The US magistrate judge Lindsay Griffin agreed on Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody.

Markle’s arrest on Friday followed the seizure of approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, Essayli said.

Among the alleged child sexual abuse material were sexually explicit photographs of Markle with underage girls, including one taken in what appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, Reuters reports.

According to the criminal complaint, the special agent investigating Markle’s alleged storage unit said he “viewed a collection of what appeared to be strips of 35mm film negatives seized from Storage Unit 1 registered to Markle”.

“To date, I have identified approximately 18 images that appeared to constitute child pornography,” the special agent noted in the complaint, adding that the investigation remains ongoing.

Markle reportedly had rented the storage units in Los Angeles since 2008, with the FBI noting that the most recent auto-payment for the units was on 14 October.

“Markle’s use of Storage Unit 1 was also corroborated by items found within the unit bearing his name, including boxes labeled ‘Tom Markle’ and an address within the central district of California,” the criminal complaint said.

During his arrest last week, he was taken from a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, by ambulance. Hours later, a judge allowed Markle to be released on the condition that he be electronically monitored, which typically means wearing an ankle tether.

According to Griffin, Markle’s court appearance last Friday included a “lack of recall”. Griffin also cited Markle’s “health condition” and “advanced age” as part of his appearance.

The judge ordered a mental competency exam and a report by 20 November.

Griffin said she found “reasonable cause to believe” Markle was suffering from a condition “rendering him mentally incompetent to the extent that he is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him or to assist properly in his defense”, CBS reported.

His daughter, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and actor who starred in the US television drama Suits.

Meghan recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”

Thomas Markle was living in the Philippines this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US.

His arrest followed reports by the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan’s half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two US storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

Associated Press contributed reporting

output.headline: What would you like to ask our writers about 2026?
output.trail: Share your questions for our live panel as the Guardian looks back on the biggest stories of the year.

output.headline: Live blog closes after House Republicans vote against Hegseth impeachment
output.trail: The Pentagon declared 'total victory' after Republicans blocked the effort to impeach Pete Hegseth; this live blog is now closed.

output.headline: Rocket attack on Iraq base leaves two Americans and one UK soldier dead
output.trail: 12 others were injured by a fusillade of Katyusha rockets; soon after, airstrikes were reported on an Iran-backed militia base.

output.headline: Brazilian prosecutors charge journalist Glenn Greenwald with cybercrimes
output.trail: Greenwald is accused of helping hackers who obtained cellphone messages between leading figures in an anti-corruption investigation.

output.headline: Netanyahu calls Israel's war in Gaza 'opposite of genocide' in UN speech
output.trail: The Israeli PM attacked critics and called New York mayor Zohran Mamdani 'antisemitic' in an inflammatory address.

output.headline: Iran and US hold talks on sidelines of UN summit, Trump says
output.trail: A senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen the strait of Hormuz if the US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran.
output.progress: Diplomatic talks between Iran and the US are under way on the sidelines of the summit.

output.headline: Trump to push for Ukraine-Russia energy ceasefire at UN meeting
output.trail: The US president is set to meet his Ukrainian counterpart in New York, as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russia's energy sector.
output.progress: Trump plans to press for an energy ceasefire when the two leaders meet.

output.headline: Trump claims US will end military aid to Israel by end of this year
output.trail: The US president made a surprise election day announcement, saying the country does not 'need' the $4bn annual payment.

output.headline: Judge dismisses Trump's $3.8bn defamation lawsuit against Washington Post
output.trail: The suit stemmed from a 2023 Post article that said a bank with ties to the porn industry helped fund Trump's media operation.
output.progress: The judge's dismissal upholds the Washington Post's reporting.

output.headline: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC lawsuit
output.trail: The judge said he would dismiss Trump's BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with the discovery process and sits for deposition.
output.progress: The judge is enforcing the discovery process to ensure Trump cooperates.

output.headline: Federal judge blocks Trump's latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship
output.trail: The Supreme Court ruled in June against the president's earlier order to change citizenship rules for babies born in the US.
output.progress: The courts have repeatedly stepped in to block the administration's attempts to restrict birthright citizenship.

output.headline: BBC pushes judge to force Trump deposition in $10bn lawsuit
output.trail: The BBC asked the US federal judge to compel Trump's lawyers to schedule a deposition after his team cancelled the initial session.
output.progress: The BBC is pressing the court to enforce the deposition after Trump's team cancelled it.

output.headline: Supreme court allows Trump's mail-in voting rules to take effect
output.trail: The justices' ruling comes after lower courts had blocked the president's election order ahead of the November midterms.

output.headline: Judge orders Trump to divulge financial details in BBC lawsuit
output.trail: The ruling could open a window into the first family's multiple business ventures, a setback for Trump in the defamation suit against the broadcaster.
output.progress: The ruling forces greater transparency about the Trump family's business ventures.

output.headline: Judge who sentenced Russell Brand praised for dispelling rape myths
output.trail: The Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hailed Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering his remarks with 'piercing clarity'.

output.headline: Brand's barrister reports himself to watchdog over clash with journalist
output.trail: Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand's victims coming forward, 'I hope you are pleased with yourself'.
output.progress: The barrister has referred his own conduct to the regulator, a sign the oversight system is working.

output.headline: From Big Brother to convicted rapist: how the system finally caught Russell Brand
output.trail: The former comedian long traded on his extreme persona, yet many will wonder how he was allowed to act in plain sight for so long.

output.headline: Brand case must be wake-up call to protect women in media, says Nandy
output.trail: The culture secretary says there is still a problem with exploitation and abuse in the industry and public life.
output.progress: Nandy is calling for stronger protections for women in media following the case.

output.headline: The Guardian view: Russell Brand's conviction sends a powerful message
output.trail: The brave women who testified against the star have helped expose the sexual entitlement that he personified, the editorial says.

output.headline: Why did Russell Brand convert to Christianity?
output.trail: Sincere or self-serving, the disgraced comedian's case shows how the church has become a culture war frontier.

output.headline: Bank of England holds rates steady, paving the way for relief ahead
output.trail: The bank held rates at 3.75% and indicates anti-inflation measures in Rachel Reeves's budget are likely to pave the way for rate cuts in the months ahead.

output.headline: Bank of England's rate pause raises hopes peak has been reached
output.trail: It offers relief for mortgage holders after 14 consecutive rises, as the UK economy comes under growing pressure.

output.headline: Bank of England forecast to lower interest rates amid rising unemployment
output.trail: The City predicts a quarter-point drop to 4% when the MPC meets on Thursday, as Trump's tariffs weigh on the economy.

output.headline: Interest rates rise again but Bank of England hints at a brighter future
output.trail: Threadneedle Street is still expecting a recession, but says it is likely to be a mild one by UK standards.

output.headline: Bank of England holds interest rates at 4% and slows bond-selling scheme
output.trail: The decision on government debt holdings could reduce market jitters and the Treasury's borrowing costs.

output.headline: UK inflation hits eight-month high of 2.6%, fuelling calls to hold interest rates
output.trail: The annual increase in November was driven by rising petrol and grocery costs and a hike in tobacco duty in the budget.

output.headline: Louise Casey takes on the challenge of fixing England's social care
output.trail: The troubleshooter for four previous prime ministers has been charged with saving the adult social care sector, after years of it being called the biggest challenge yet.
output.progress: Casey has been given the task of fixing the system.

output.headline: Louise Casey's review pushes for reckoning on social care
output.trail: The head of the government-commissioned review says adult social care is held together by 'sticking plasters and glue'.
output.progress: The review is pressing for a reckoning that could lead to lasting reform.

output.headline: Nearly 100,000 adults in England go without state-funded social care
output.trail: The number of people receiving subsidised care has fallen far more quickly than the country's disability rate, after cuts to funding, analysis finds.

output.headline: Age UK says social care services across England face extreme duress
output.trail: The charity says services for older and sick people in some areas could fail without more funding.

output.headline: MPs call for at least £7bn a year more for social care
output.trail: The full cost of adequately funding the sector is likely to run into tens of billions, the committee says.
output.progress: MPs are calling on the government to invest at least £7bn a year more.

output.headline: Cross-party committee urges extra £8bn investment in social care
output.trail: A cross-party committee says over a million vulnerable older people have been left without support.
output.progress: Peers are calling for an extra £8bn to address the shortfall.

output.headline: What to know about the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
output.trail: Hegseth is facing a Republican-led impeachment effort accusing him of violating federal law and the constitution.

output.headline: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war
output.trail: The congressman says the defense secretary repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war.
output.progress: Massie is pursuing impeachment in response to the alleged violations.

output.headline: Trump's controversial Pentagon pick Pete Hegseth confirmed by Senate
output.trail: The vice-president cast the tie-breaking vote for the Fox News host, despite allegations of sexual assault and alcohol abuse.

output.headline: Hegseth grilled by Democrats over sexual assault and drinking claims
output.trail: Trump's Pentagon pick testified 'I'm not perfect' at his Senate confirmation hearing amid concerns over his personal history.
output.progress: Senators pressed Hegseth directly on the allegations during the hearing.

output.headline: Collins and Tillis break ranks to oppose Hegseth's censure of Kelly
output.trail: Their pushback is striking amid a tepid response from most other Republican senators to the censure of fellow senator Mark Kelly.
output.progress: The two senators publicly broke with their party to oppose the censure.

output.headline: Rise of Palestinian parties could redraw Israel's political landscape
output.trail: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing.

output.headline: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel's PM
output.trail: Opposition politicians get their first chance to take control of the levers of power, even as they struggle to form a government.

output.headline: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
output.trail: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vowed 'to destroy this place' in retaliation for a militant attack on an army checkpoint.

output.headline: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
output.trail: Democrats' sweep could encourage Israel's divided opposition to join forces and remove the prime minister closely allied with Trump.

output.headline: Rescue teams dig through rubble in Gaza City after building falls, killing 21
output.trail: Rescue workers say the search for dozens of people is hampered by a lack of heavy machinery.
output.progress: Rescue teams are searching for dozens of people still missing beneath the rubble.

output.headline: Major Israeli TV networks revise polling projections – as it happened
output.trail: This blog has now closed.

output.headline: Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, charged in Florida in connection to child sexual abuse material
output.trail: The father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said.

output.headline: California to 'actively monitor' for threats after Trump's Iran remarks
output.trail: Gavin Newsom said the state's threat-assessment centre would be on heightened alert after the president's remarks that Iran could 'take out' LA and San Diego.
output.progress: California has put its threat-assessment centre on heightened alert in response.

output.headline: Trump 'happy' about Harry and Meghan's UK return: 'I was not a fan'
output.trail: The president praised the late queen and King Charles but said the duke and duchess treated the royal family 'with great disrespect'.

output.headline: California man rescued alive after 30 days stranded at sea
output.trail: Kai Sato used PVC pipes and kayak paddles to try to repair his boat, and a plastic bag to collect condensation to drink, before his rescue.

output.headline: Southern California swelters as late-season heatwave smothers region
output.trail: Temperatures are expected to hover around 100F in downtown LA and even hotter inland, raising concerns about wildfires.

output.headline: The ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California's proposed billionaire tax
output.trail: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that would fund healthcare and education.

output.headline: Medical breakthrough offers hope to people with same condition as Céline Dion
output.trail: Some patients with the autoimmune condition in the trial have been able to return to work and resume hobbies.
output.progress: Researchers' trial findings mean treatment advances are already helping patients regain function.

output.headline: Australia's 'forest fairies' get a new neighbourhood to help them bounce back
output.trail: With only a handful of lowland Leadbeater's possums left in Victorian forests, conservationists hope the bespoke sanctuary will help the acrobatic marsupials recover.
output.progress: Conservationists have built a bespoke sanctuary to help the possums bounce back.

output.headline: Rediscovered medieval stained glass goes on view at Coventry cathedral after 90 years
output.trail: Remnants of 15th-century artwork form a treasure trove that can now be viewed for the first time in almost 90 years, pieced together like a medieval jigsaw puzzle.

output.headline: Erling Haaland donates rare £100k Viking history book to Norwegian library
output.trail: The Manchester City footballer and his father gave the rare 16th-century edition of Viking royal sagas to the library in Bryne, his hometown.

output.headline: For the first time in 160 years, Sheffield's lost river comes back into view
output.trail: The River Sheaf, which gave the city its name, can now be glimpsed by train passengers beneath their feet at Sheffield station.
